title: Holiday ideas when you can't decide where to go
intro: Staring at a blank search box? Here are nine ways to find your next holiday, from starting with the month to picking a trip you've already loved and doing it differently.
seo_title: Can't decide where to go on holiday? 9 ways to find ideas

sections.heading: Why it's hard to think of anywhere
sections.text:
When you can go anywhere, it's surprisingly hard to think of somewhere. Too much choice makes every option feel equally good, or equally risky, and you end up going back to the same place as last year.

The trick is to stop asking "where should we go?" and start somewhere narrower. Pick one starting point below, and you'll have a shortlist in minutes.

sections.heading: 1. Start with the month
sections.text:
If your dates are fixed, start with where's at its best then. It rules out a lot of places straight away (nobody wants Marrakech in August or Tromsø in June) and points you at places you might never have thought of.

Our month pages list the places at their best in each month:
- [Where to go in February](/destinations/where-to-go-in-february), for half term sun or snow
- [Where to go in May](/destinations/where-to-go-in-may), before the summer crowds
- [Where to go in August](/destinations/where-to-go-in-august), for the summer holidays
- [Where to go in October](/destinations/where-to-go-in-october), for autumn half term

sections.heading: 2. Start with the kind of trip
sections.text:
Decide what kind of holiday you want before you decide where. A beach, a city, mountains, a road trip or somewhere to do absolutely nothing are very different holidays, and each one narrows the map.

Browse by type: [beach holidays](/destinations/beach-holidays), [city breaks](/destinations/city-breaks), [nature holidays](/destinations/nature-holidays), [road trips](/destinations/road-trips) or [relaxing holidays](/destinations/relaxing-holidays).

sections.heading: 3. Start with how far you'll travel
sections.text: Set a limit on the journey, like "no more than three hours on a plane" or "somewhere we can drive to". That one rule turns the whole world into a short list. A short journey matters more than people expect with small children, or on a long weekend.

sections.heading: 4. Start with what you loved last time
sections.text: Think about the best holiday you've had. What made it? If it was the food in Italy, try [Puglia](/destinations/puglia) or [Syracuse](/destinations/syracuse). If it was the mountains in Austria, try [Ljubljana](/destinations/ljubljana) or [Annecy](/destinations/annecy). Somewhere similar but new is often a safer bet than somewhere completely different.

sections.heading: 5. Do the opposite of last time
sections.text: Or go the other way. If last year was a busy city break, make this one a quiet island. If it was a fortnight by a pool, try a road trip. A change is half the point of a holiday, and it's a good way to give someone who didn't love last year's trip their turn.

sections.heading: 6. Follow a food, a film or a book
sections.text: Plenty of great holidays start with "I've always wanted to try…" or "remember that film set in…". Ask everyone for one thing they'd love to eat, see or do, then find where it is. Pasta-making, the northern lights, a safari, a road trip from a favourite film: any of them is a good place to start.

sections.heading: 7. Look at somewhere's neighbour
sections.text: Love the idea of Santorini or Venice but not the crowds or prices? Look next door. Smaller islands like [Naxos](/destinations/naxos) and [Milos](/destinations/milos), or cities like [Ghent](/destinations/ghent) instead of Bruges, often give you the same feel for less money and with more room.

sections.heading: 8. Ask everyone for one idea
sections.text: If you're choosing as a family or a group, don't do all the thinking yourself. Ask everyone for one place, however unlikely. You'll end up with a more interesting list than you'd make alone, and everyone will care more about the result. Our post on [agreeing on a holiday as a family](/blog/how-to-agree-on-a-holiday-as-a-family) has more on this.

sections.heading: 9. Leave the final choice to chance
sections.text: If you've got a list but can't pick, let a draw choose. Put three to six ideas in, give everyone some points to spread, and let the draw pick, with the most popular places having the best chance. It's quicker than another week of debate, and it's surprisingly exciting. See [fair ways to pick a holiday](/blog/fair-ways-to-pick-a-holiday) for how it works.

faqs.question: What do you do when you can't decide where to go on holiday?
faqs.answer: Narrow the question. Start from your dates, the kind of trip you want or how far you'll travel, make a shortlist of three to six places, then use points and a draw to pick one.

faqs.question: How do I get holiday ideas?
faqs.answer: Look at where's at its best in the month you're going, browse by the kind of holiday you want, think about what you loved on your favourite past trip, or ask everyone going for one idea each.

faqs.question: Where should I go on holiday if I've never been abroad?
faqs.answer: Somewhere with a short flight, easy transport and plenty to do is a good first trip, such as Lisbon, Barcelona, Valencia or Malta. They're all about three hours or less from much of the UK.
